label: lem:integral-negative-boundary-matching
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:integral-negative-boundary-matching}
The following statements hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item For distinct negative boundaries \(B_i,B_j\),
\[
 [B_i]+[B_j]=[B_{\pi(i)}]+[B_{\pi(j)}]
 \quad\text{in }H_1(S;\mathbb F_2).
\]
If there are at least four negative boundaries, every negative block
is fixed unless \(b=4\) and every boundary is negative. In that case
\(\pi\) belongs to the Klein four group.
\item If there are exactly two negative boundaries and at least two
positive boundaries, then both negative blocks are fixed.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For a negative boundary, let \(Q_i\subset K_{\mathbb Q}\) be its
canonical sum of non-trivial primary spaces. A local generator at an
endpoint \(x\) gives a collar class \(q_x\), the negative half of the
twisted boundary loop based at \(x\), with endpoint coefficient \(x\).
Thus \(Q_i\) maps isomorphically to its endpoint block.
Projection of \(K\) to \(Q_i\) gives a lattice
\(\Lambda_i\cong\mathbb Z^{m_i}\). Its intersection
\(\Lambda_i^{\mathrm{ev}}=Q_i\cap K\) consists of the vectors with even
total coefficient. Hence
\(\Lambda_i/\Lambda_i^{\mathrm{ev}}\cong\mathbb F_2\).
The assertion follows directly from the relative chain complex of
the negative-holonomy circle. Boundary loops have endpoint coefficient
\(\pm2\), while paths between endpoints give signed differences.
Projection realizes an odd coordinate because another boundary can
supply the second odd endpoint. Both lattices are intrinsic.

For two negative blocks choose \(v_i\in\Lambda_i\) and
\(v_j\in\Lambda_j\) with odd parity. There is an integral
class \(x\in K\) with these endpoint coordinates and no others.
The image of the endpoint map is the even-total lattice, as
\(H_0(S;L_{\mathbb Z})=\mathbb Z/2\). Write
\[
 a=2x-2v_i-2v_j\in A_{\mathbb Z}.
\]
Its class \(\delta_{ij}\in A_{\mathbb Z}/2A_{\mathbb Z}\) is
independent of all choices. For another choice
\(x',v_i',v_j'\), the differences \(v_i'-v_i\) and
\(v_j'-v_j\) lie in \(\Lambda_i^{\mathrm{ev}}\) and
\(\Lambda_j^{\mathrm{ev}}\). They are integral, and
cancellation of the endpoint coordinates gives
\[
 x'-x-(v_i'-v_i)-(v_j'-v_j)\in A_{\mathbb Z}.
\]
The two resulting absolute classes therefore differ by an element of
\(2A_{\mathbb Z}\). An integral intertwiner carries \(\delta_{ij}\) to the
corresponding class for the permuted blocks.

Reduction of the twisted chain complex modulo two gives the ordinary
chain complex. Since \(H_0(S;L_{\mathbb Z})\simeq\mathbb Z/2\), the universal
coefficient sequence is
\[
 0\longrightarrow A_{\mathbb Z}/2A_{\mathbb Z}
 \longrightarrow H_1(S;\mathbb F_2)
 \longrightarrow
 \operatorname{Tor}_1^{\mathbb Z}(H_0(S;L_{\mathbb Z}),\mathbb F_2)
 \longrightarrow0.
\]
The class of \(2x\) reduces to zero, while \(2v_i\) and \(2v_j\) reduce
to the two ordinary boundary loops.
Consequently \(\delta_{ij}\)
maps to \([B_i]+[B_j]\). The injection in the displayed universal
coefficient sequence is essential here. In particular, one must not
identify \(A_{\mathbb Z}/2A_{\mathbb Z}\) with all of \(H_1(S;\mathbb F_2)\), since the
final Tor term is non-zero. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:absolute-intertwiner-scalar}, the absolute intertwiner
is \(\pm f_*\). Naturality of the displayed injection therefore
identifies the two boundary sums. The common sign disappears modulo
two, giving the asserted identity.

Over \(\mathbb F_2\), the boundary classes have the single relation
\(\sum_i[B_i]=0\). If \(b\ne4\) and there
are at least four negative boundaries, equality of two sums of
distinct pairs forces equality of the unordered pairs. A permutation
of at least three elements fixing every unordered pair is the
identity.

For \(b=4\), a pair may instead be replaced by its
complement. The permutations preserving the three partitions into
complementary pairs form the Klein four group. This proves
\textup{(i)}.

By Proposition~\ref{prop:geometric-boundary-matching}, the positive
boundaries have matching stop numbers. Identify their stop sets by
isotopies in boundary collars. Multiplying the intertwiner by a common
sign, we may assume
\(
 \Theta|_{A_{\mathbb Q}}=I\). Write \(b_+\) for the number of positive boundary components.
Write \(B^-_1,B^-_2\) for the negative boundaries and
\(B^+_1,\ldots,B^+_{b_+}\) for the positive boundaries. Denote the
positive boundary classes by \(d_1,\ldots,d_{b_+}\), and set
\[
 R=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q}\{d_1,\ldots,d_{b_+}\}.
\]
The classes \(d_i\) are independent by
Lemma~\ref{lem:twisted-homology-normal-forms}.

Set \(F=\operatorname{Stab}_{\operatorname{Mod}(S,\partial S)}(\eta)\).
Proposition~\ref{prop:represented-boundary-data} identifies the
boundary-pointwise stabilizers. After the geometric transport, the
induced isomorphism on their common underlying group \(F\) has the form
\[
 y\longmapsto yz(y),
 \qquad z(y)=\prod_B T_B^{n_B(y)}.
\]
Here \(B\) ranges over the boundary components and
\(n_B(y)\in\mathbb Z\).
Indeed, the two maps have the same image after the stops are forgotten,
while their difference on \(F\) lies in the central lattice generated
by the full boundary twists.
The full twists, with the complement-fixed normalization of
Lemma~\ref{lem:normalized-twisted-collar}, act trivially on absolute
twisted homology. Since \(\Theta|_{A_{\mathbb Q}}=I\), the equivariance equation has no
additional common sign when the same local-system lift of \(y\) is
used on both sides.

We now prove that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:two-negative-fixed-totals}
 \lambda_i\Theta=\lambda_i
 \qquad\text{ for }1\leq i\leq b_+,
\end{equation}
where \(\lambda_i\) is the endpoint total at the \(i\)-th positive
boundary \(B_i^+\). Let \(\beta\) be a
positive-holonomy nonseparating curve with nonradical twisted class.
Choose a negative-holonomy partner meeting it once, as in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:separating-twisted-scalar-commutant}. The boundary
\(\gamma\) of their regular neighbourhood is separating. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:twisted-picard-lefschetz}, its twist acts on relative
homology as
\[
 I+N_\beta,
 \qquad N_\beta=a_\beta[\beta]\otimes\lambda_\beta,
 \qquad a_\beta\neq0,
\]
where \(\lambda_\beta\) is the twisted intersection covector. This action
is the identity on the endpoint quotient.

The image of \(T_\gamma\) under the represented isomorphism must also
act identically on that quotient. The negative-boundary exponents in
\(z(T_\gamma)\) are therefore even, and their relative actions are
trivial by Lemma~\ref{lem:normalized-twisted-collar}. The remaining
central correction has the form
\[
 I+D,
 \qquad
 D=\varepsilon_\partial\sum_i n_i d_i\otimes\lambda_i,\qquad
 n_i\in\mathbb Z.
\]
Since \(N_\beta D=DN_\beta=0\) and \(\Theta N_\beta=N_\beta\), expansion
of the equivariance equation gives
\[
 N_\beta-N_\beta\Theta=D\Theta.
\]
The left-hand side has image in \(\mathbb Q[\beta]\), while the right-hand
side has image in \(R\). These spaces intersect trivially because
\([\beta]\) is nonradical. Hence, we have
\(\lambda_\beta\Theta=\lambda_\beta\).

Band-sum \(\beta\) with \(B_i^+\). The resulting
curve is positive-holonomy and nonseparating, with class
\([\beta]\pm d_i\). The same argument applies to it. With compatible choices of signs, the
twisted intersection pairing gives
\[
 \lambda_{\beta\pm d_i}=\lambda_\beta\pm\lambda_i.
\] Subtracting the invariant
covectors proves \eqref{eq:two-negative-fixed-totals}.

Let \(M_+^\circ\) be the set of endpoints on positive boundaries and put
\[
 C_-=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q}\{r_i:\nu_i=-1\}
 \subset C_{\mathbb Q}.
\]
The collar
decomposition and Lemma~\ref{lem:normalized-twisted-collar} identify
\[
 K_{+,\mathbb Q}
 =K_{\mathbb Q}^{C\cap C_-}
 =H_1(S,M_+^\circ;L).
\]
The action on this fixed subspace factors through
\(C/(C\cap C_-)\). Let \(V_0\) be the simultaneous generalized
trivial-character subspace for this quotient action. This definition
is intrinsic and does not require a choice of lifts of the positive
quotient axes to \(C\). In particular, the represented intertwiner
carries \(V_0\) to its target counterpart. Collar rotations commute
with the \(F\)-action, so \(V_0\) is an \(F\)-submodule. It fits into
\[
 0\longrightarrow A_{\mathbb Q}
 \longrightarrow V_0
 \xrightarrow{(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_{b_+})}
 \mathbb Q^{b_+}\longrightarrow0.
\]
The positive endpoint sets have already been identified. The inclusion
of pairs therefore identifies both copies of \(K_{+,\mathbb Q}\) with
the same \(H_1(S,M_+^\circ;L)\), including their uncorrected \(F\)-actions
and the subspace \(V_0\). The actual actions differ only by the central
boundary corrections above. Together with
\(\Theta|_{A_{\mathbb Q}}=I\), equation
\eqref{eq:two-negative-fixed-totals} now gives
\[
 \Theta|_{V_0}=I+\Delta,
 \qquad \Delta|_{A_{\mathbb Q}}=0,
 \qquad \Delta(V_0)\subseteq A_{\mathbb Q}.
\]

The normal form in
Lemma~\ref{lem:twisted-homology-normal-forms} gives a
non-degenerate \(2g\)-dimensional handle complement to \(R\). The
restrictions to \(A_{\mathbb Q}\) of the intersection covectors
of its positive-holonomy handle curves have common annihilator \(R\).
Their invariance under \(\Theta\) therefore
implies \(\Delta(V_0)\subseteq R\). Write
\[
 \Delta=\sum_{i,j}\Delta_{ij}d_i\otimes\lambda_j.
\]

For \(y\in F\), let \(\mu_i(y)\in\{1,-1\}\) be its coefficient sign
at the \(i\)-th positive boundary. Naturality gives
\[
 y_*d_i=\mu_i(y)d_i,
 \qquad \lambda_i y_*=\mu_i(y)\lambda_i.
\]
On \(V_0\), a central correction has the form \(I+D_y\), with
\(D_y\) in the span of the diagonal operators
\(d_i\otimes\lambda_i\). Since both \(D_y\) and \(\Delta\) vanish on
absolute homology, the equivariance equation gives
\[
 \Delta y_*-y_*\Delta=y_*D_y.
\]
Its off-diagonal coefficients satisfy
\[
 \bigl(\mu_j(y)-\mu_i(y)\bigr)\Delta_{ij}=0
 \qquad\text{ for }i\neq j.
\]

For each \(i\), choose a separating curve enclosing \(B^-_1\) and
\(B_i^+\), and no other boundary component. Its
holonomy is negative. Normalize the local-system lift of its twist
to be the identity on the side containing the other positive boundaries.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:twisted-picard-lefschetz}, this gives
\(\mu_i=-1\) and \(\mu_j=1\) for \(j\neq i\). Changing the lift
changes all signs at once and does not affect the displayed equation.

For a fixed ordered pair \(i\ne j\), this choice gives
\(\mu_j-\mu_i=2\), up to a common sign. Over \(\mathbb Q\), the coefficient equation therefore forces \(\Delta_{ij}=0\).
Varying \(i\) eliminates every off-diagonal coefficient. Consequently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:two-negative-diagonal-correction}
 \Theta|_{V_0}=I+\sum_i a_i d_i\otimes\lambda_i.
\end{equation}

We now retain the integral information. Use the two-negative normal
form in \eqref{eq:two-negative-absolute-normal-form} and write
\[
 c_2-c_1=d_1+\cdots+d_{b_+}=:d,
 \qquad
 A_{\mathbb Z}=H_{\mathbb Z}\oplus\bigoplus_{i=1}^{b_+}\mathbb Z d_i.
\]
Choose the collar coordinates \(q_x\) from
Lemma~\ref{lem:integral-collar-gluing} with
\(B^-_1\) as the base boundary. 
An expression with absolute part
\(a\in A_{\mathbb Q}\) and endpoint coefficients \(n_x\) is integral
if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:two-negative-integral-lattice}
 n_x\in\mathbb Z,
 \qquad \sum_xn_x\in2\mathbb Z,
 \qquad a-\frac{n^-_2}{2}d\in A_{\mathbb Z},
 \qquad n^-_2=\sum_{x\in M^\circ\cap B^-_2}n_x.
\end{equation}

Let \(Q_k\) be the canonical negative block at \(B^-_k\). Projection of
\(K\) to \(Q_k\) gives
\[
 \Lambda_k=\bigoplus_{x\in M^\circ\cap B^-_k}\mathbb Z q_x,
 \qquad
 Q_k\cap K=
 \left\{\sum_{x\in M^\circ\cap B^-_k}n_xq_x\ \middle|\
             \sum_{x\in M^\circ\cap B^-_k}n_x\in2\mathbb Z\right\}.
\]
These are the intrinsic lattices from the first part of the proof. If \(\Theta\) exchanges
\(Q_1\) and \(Q_2\), the image of any \(q_x\) with
\(x\in M^\circ\cap B^-_1\)
has integral coordinates and odd total coefficient in \(Q_2\).

It remains to control the extra endpoints on a positive boundary. Let
\(W_j\) be the sum of the non-trivial primary spaces of its rotation.
For two endpoints \(y,y'\) on \(B_j^+\), set
\[
 U_j=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q}
 \{d_j,\ q_y-q_{y'}\mid y,y'\in M^\circ\cap B_j^+\}.
\]
The full twist is trivial on \(U_j\), so the one-step rotation
has finite order there and is semisimple. Its endpoint quotient
is the zero-total cyclic module, which has no invariant vector.
Hence its invariant subspace is exactly \(\mathbb Qd_j\).
Consequently,
\(
 U_j=\mathbb Qd_j\oplus W_j\). In particular, \(W_j\) has no absolute boundary coordinate along
\(d_i\) for \(i\neq j\). Decompose
\(q_y=v_y+w_y\), with \(v_y\in V_0\) and \(w_y\in W_j\). The vector
\(v_y\) has endpoint-total vector equal to the \(j\)-th standard
basis vector. The positive block at \(B_j^+\) has already been matched,
so \(\Theta(W_j)=W_j\). Equation
\eqref{eq:two-negative-diagonal-correction} now gives
\(
 \Theta q_y-q_y\in U_j\). Thus \(\Theta q_y\) has total endpoint coefficient one on \(B_j^+\), no
endpoint coefficients on the other positive boundaries, and no
absolute coordinate along \(d_i\) for \(i\neq j\).

Choose \(x\in M^\circ\cap B^-_1\) and an endpoint \(y\) on \(B_j^+\).
The vector
\(q_x+q_y\) is integral by
\eqref{eq:two-negative-integral-lattice}. If the negative blocks were
exchanged, its image would have odd total coefficient on \(B^-_2\).
The same integral lattice condition would force its absolute
coefficient along every \(d_i\) to be \(1/2\) modulo \(\mathbb Z\). For
\(i\neq j\), the preceding arguments show that this coefficient is
zero. Such an \(i\) exists because \(b_+\geq2\). This contradiction
proves that the negative blocks cannot be exchanged, completing
\textup{(ii)}.

label: lem:normalized-representation-extension
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:normalized-representation-extension}
Suppose that \(\phi:H_\eta\to H_{\eta'}\) is an isomorphism and that
\(\Theta:K(\mathbb S)\to K(\mathbb S')\) intertwines the normalized
stabilizer representations. If there is an isomorphism
\(h:H_1(S;\mathbb Z)\to H_1(S';\mathbb Z)\) satisfying
\(hy_*=\phi(y)_*h\) for every \(y\in H_\eta\), then \((\phi,\Theta)\)
extends to a shift-preserving isomorphism of represented invariants.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The non-zero windings eliminate the additive factors in the
geometrisation kernel of Theorem~\ref{thm:opper-geometrization}.
Normalization at the fixed stop splits the grading extension.
Choose a splitting of the geometrisation sequence and restrict it
to the normalized copy of \(H_\eta\) in the graded mapping class
group. Together with the actual central shift \([1]\), this gives
the displayed decomposition of \(D(\mathbb S)\). We also make the same
choices for \(\mathbb S'\).
Define
\[
 h^\vee:H^1(S;\mathbf{k}^\times)\longrightarrow H^1(S';\mathbf{k}^\times),
 \qquad h^\vee(\chi)=\chi\circ h^{-1}.
\]
The assumed ordinary homological equivariance makes \(h^\vee\)
equivariant for \(\phi\). It therefore extends \(\phi\) to the
semidirect products in the displayed decomposition. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:geometrization-charge-action}, the local-system torus
acts trivially on the charge lattices, while the shift acts by \(-I\). Sending
\((\chi,y,n)\) to \((h^\vee(\chi),\phi(y),n)\) and using \(\Theta\)
on the charge lattice gives the required represented isomorphism.

label: lem:exceptional-representation-calculations
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:exceptional-representation-calculations}
In each of the following cases, the formula for \(\phi\) defines an
isomorphism of the stopped line-field stabilizers and admits an integral
intertwiner of the normalized charge representations:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item the two-boundary construction of
Example~\ref{ex:two-boundary-represented-failure};
\item the three-boundary construction of
Example~\ref{ex:three-boundary-represented-failure};
\item the four-boundary construction of
Example~\ref{ex:four-boundary-represented-failure}.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, the two represented invariants in each example are
isomorphic.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We retain the notation of the respective examples. In each case the
source \(\mathbb S\) and target \(\mathbb S'\) have the same underlying
surface and orientation local system, and we use common notation for
absolute homology. With the line fields, stop counts, characters, and
explicit formulas specified there, we verify the root relations and
integral equivariance separately in each case.

In all three cases, the central correction on \(F\) is invertible.
Its defining characters vanish on the correcting central elements,
so negating the correction exponents gives the inverse. We also check
the root relations and the induced maps on the finite quotients by \(F\).

\medskip
\noindent\emph{Proof of \textup{(i):} two boundary components.}
The root relation is preserved because
\[
 \phi(\rho_2)^m=T_1^{-q^2}T_2^{2m}=\alpha(T_2).
\]
On the quotient by \(F\), the map is multiplication by
\(-q^2\equiv-1\pmod m\), so it is an isomorphism. It induces the
identity after the boundary twists are forgotten and hence on ordinary
homology.

The orientation local system is positive on the handles and negative
on both boundaries. Equation~\eqref{eq:two-negative-absolute-normal-form}
then shows that the two negative boundary chains agree.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:integral-collar-gluing}, after exchanging the source
and target boundary blocks, both charge lattices have the model
\[
 K=A_{\mathbb Z}\oplus
 \left\{\sum_x n_xq_x:n_x\in\mathbb Z,\quad
                         \sum_x n_x\equiv0\pmod2\right\}.
\]
Normalize source lifts at the unique stop on \(B_1\) and target lifts
at the unique stop on \(B_2\). For \(y\in F\), relative displacement gives the signs
\[
 \begin{array}{c|cc}
  &B_1&B_2\\\hline
  \text{source}&1&(-1)^{\beta(y)}\\
  \text{target}&(-1)^{\beta(y)}&1.
 \end{array}
\]
The lift of \(k\) which is the identity off its boundary collars changes
both endpoint signs and fixes absolute homology. After normalization it
acts by \(-I\) on absolute homology and trivially on the endpoint
blocks. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:relative-displacement}, changing the normalization of \(y\) from \(B_1\) to \(B_2\)
multiplies its absolute action by \((-1)^{\beta(y)}\). The factor \(k^{\beta(y)}\)
contributes the same sign and cancels this discrepancy. Thus the target
action of \(\alpha(y)\) agrees with the source action of \(y\) on
absolute homology, while the two endpoint sign characters agree after
exchanging the blocks. Choose cyclic bases
\(e_0,\ldots,e_{m-1}\) and \(e'_0,\ldots,e'_{m-1}\) for the non-trivial
source and target root blocks, and denote the corresponding signed cycles
by \(R\) and \(R'\). Then \(R^m=(R')^m=-I\). Since
\(q^2\equiv1\pmod{2m}\), its target image acts as \((R')^{-1}\).
The signed reversal
\[
 e_0\longmapsto e'_0,
 \qquad e_j\longmapsto-e'_{m-j}\quad\text{ for }1\leq j<m
\]
intertwines these cycles. Exchanging the two endpoint blocks by this
map, and taking the identity on \(A_{\mathbb Z}\), preserves the even-total
lattice. Lemma~\ref{lem:normalized-representation-extension} gives the
required isomorphism of represented invariants.

\medskip
\noindent\emph{Proof of \textup{(ii):} three boundary components.}
Here
\[
 \phi(\rho_2)^m=T_1^{-q}T_2^{2m}=\alpha(T_2),
 \qquad -q\equiv1\pmod m.
\]
The map is therefore an isomorphism. Its matrix on the first two
rotation directions has determinant
\(2m(1-q)+q^2=1\), and it fixes the third direction.

Let \(c_1,c_2\) be the two negative boundary chains and put
\(d=c_2-c_1=[B_3]_L\), up to the common collar convention. Write
\[
 A_{\mathbb Z}=H_{\mathbb Z}\oplus\mathbb Z d,
 \qquad
 K_{\mathbb Q}=H_{\mathbb Q}\oplus\mathbb Qd
       \oplus\mathbb Qz\oplus E_1\oplus E_2,
\]
for the source, where \(H_{\mathbb Q}=H_{\mathbb Z}\otimes\mathbb Q\). The
target has the analogous decomposition with \(E_1\) and \(E_2\)
exchanged. Choose the source collar coordinates
\(q_x\) from Lemma~\ref{lem:integral-collar-gluing} with \(B_1\) as
the base boundary. Here
\[
 E_i=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb Q}
 \{q_x:x\in M^\circ\cap B_i\}
 \quad\text{ for }i=1,2,
\]
and \(x_3\) is the unique endpoint on \(B_3\), with collar coordinate
\(z=q_{x_3}\).
An element of \(K_{\mathbb Q}\) has a unique expression
\[
 x_H+ad+n_3z+
 \sum_{x\in (M^\circ\cap B_1)\sqcup(M^\circ\cap B_2)}n_xq_x,
 \qquad
 x_H\in H_{\mathbb Q},\quad a,n_3,n_x\in\mathbb Q.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:integral-collar-gluing} shows that this element is
integral exactly when
\begin{equation}\label{eq:three-boundary-integral-conditions}
 \begin{gathered}
 x_H\in H_{\mathbb Z},\qquad n_3,n_x\in\mathbb Z,\qquad
 n_1+n_2+n_3\equiv0\pmod2,\\
 a-\frac{n_2}{2}\in\mathbb Z,
 \qquad n_i=\sum_{x\in M^\circ\cap B_i}n_x\quad\text{ for }i=1,2.
 \end{gathered}
\end{equation}
Normalize both sides at the endpoint on \(B_3\). The lift of
\(k=T_1^{-1}T_2\) is \(-I\) on \(E_1\oplus E_2\) and the identity on
\(
 U=H_{\mathbb Q}\oplus\mathbb Qd\oplus\mathbb Qz\), which is the image of
\(H_1(S,\{x_3\};L)\). The two inclusions are \(F\)-equivariant for
the common normalization, so the source and target actions agree on
\(U\). For \(y\in F\), let \(\delta_i(y)\) be the scalar by which this
normalized lift acts on \(E_i\). Relative displacement gives
\(\delta_1(y)\delta_2(y)=(-1)^{h(y)}\). Since \(q\) is odd, the factor
\(k^{qh(y)}\) exchanges the two endpoint sign characters. The full
twist at \(B_3\) has the form \(I+N_3\), where
\[
 N_3(z)=\varepsilon_\partial d,
 \qquad N_3(H_{\mathbb Q}\oplus\mathbb Qd)=0.
\]
It commutes with the stabilizer action. Since
\(\varepsilon_\partial^2=1\), the operator
\(I+\varepsilon_\partial N_3/2\) fixes
\(H_{\mathbb Q}\oplus\mathbb Qd\) and sends \(z\) to \(z+d/2\).
Composing it with the exchange of \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) therefore
intertwines \(F\) with \(\alpha(F)\). On the coordinates in
\eqref{eq:three-boundary-integral-conditions}, it sends
\[
 (n_1,n_2,n_3,a)\longmapsto(n_2,n_1,n_3,a+n_3/2).
\]
The even-total condition shows that this map and its inverse are
integral. Let \(E'_1\) be the target endpoint block at \(B_1\). The root
actions on \(E_2\) and \(E'_1\) are signed cycles \(R,R'\) with
\(R^m=(R')^m=-I\), and
\[
 \varrho_{\mathbb S'}\bigl(\phi(\rho_2)\bigr)|_{E'_1}
 =(R')^{-q}=R'.
\]
Thus the root actions are also intertwined. The coarse homological
action is unchanged, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:normalized-representation-extension} applies.

\medskip
\noindent\emph{Proof of \textup{(iii):} four boundary components.}
The root relations follow from \(1+q_m=2m\) and \(1-q_n=-2n\).
The induced maps on the cyclic quotients are invertible because
\[
 q_m^2\equiv1\pmod{2m},
 \qquad q_n^2\equiv1\pmod{2n}.
\]
Thus \(\phi\) is an isomorphism and induces the identity on the
common image of the two stabilizers in \(\operatorname{Mod}(S)\).

Choose a core vertex \(v\) and negative boundary chains with
\[
 c_4=c_1-c_2+c_3,
 \qquad \partial c_i=-2v.
\]
For
\(x\in M^\circ\cap B_i\), write \(i(x)=i\) and choose the collar
coordinate \(q_x\) from Lemma~\ref{lem:integral-collar-gluing}
with \(B_1\) as the base boundary. For endpoint coordinates
\(\mathbf n=(n_x)\), put
\[
 \Lambda_{\mathrm{ev}}=
 \left\{\mathbf n\in\mathbb Z^{M^\circ}:\sum_xn_x\equiv0\pmod2\right\},
 \qquad
 \Gamma(\mathbf n)=\frac12\sum_xn_x(c_{i(x)}-c_1).
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:integral-collar-gluing} identifies the charge lattice as
\begin{equation}\label{eq:four-negative-integral-gluing}
 K=\left\{a+\sum_xn_xq_x:\begin{array}{l}
 a\in A_{\mathbb Q},\quad \mathbf n\in\Lambda_{\mathrm{ev}},\\
 a-\Gamma(\mathbf n)\in A_{\mathbb Z}
 \end{array}\right\}.
\end{equation}
Let \(\Gamma'\) be the corresponding correction term for the target,
again based at \(B_1\). Its charge lattice has the same form with
\(\Gamma\) replaced by \(\Gamma'\).
For \(\pi=(12)(34)\), let \(\bar c_i\) denote the class represented by
the reduction of \(c_i\) in \(H_1(S;\mathbb F_2)\). Then
\[
 \bar c_{\pi(i)}-\bar c_i=\bar c_1+\bar c_2
 \qquad\text{for every }i.
\]
Let \(\Pi\) be any signed source-to-target endpoint permutation inducing
\(\pi\). Since
vectors in \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{ev}}\) have even total, we have
\[
 2\bigl(\Gamma'(\Pi\mathbf n)-\Gamma(\mathbf n)\bigr)
 \equiv
 \left(\sum_x n_x\right)(\bar c_1+\bar c_2)=0\pmod2.
\]
The integral chain on the left is a cycle which vanishes in
\(H_1(S;\mathbb F_2)\). The universal coefficient injection
\[
 A_{\mathbb Z}/2A_{\mathbb Z}\longrightarrow H_1(S;\mathbb F_2)
\]
therefore shows that
\(2(\Gamma'(\Pi\mathbf n)-\Gamma(\mathbf n))\in2A_{\mathbb Z}\). Thus
\(\Gamma'(\Pi\mathbf n)-\Gamma(\mathbf n)\in A_{\mathbb Z}\), and \(\Pi\),
extended by the identity on \(A_{\mathbb Q}\), carries the source lattice
in \eqref{eq:four-negative-integral-gluing} onto the target lattice.

Since all four boundaries are negative, there is an \(F\)-stable
decomposition
\[
 K_{\mathbb Q}=A_{\mathbb Q}\oplus Q_1\oplus Q_2\oplus Q_3\oplus Q_4.
\]
For \(y\in F\), choose one of its two lifts to \(L\) and use it in both
representations. Let \(s_i(y)\in\{1,-1\}\) be its boundary sign on
\(Q_i\). The complement-fixed lifts of \(k_{12}\) and
\(k_{34}\) have sign vectors
\[
 (-1,-1,1,1),
 \qquad (1,1,-1,-1).
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:relative-displacement} then gives
\[
 (-1)^{h_{12}(y)}=s_1(y)s_2(y),
 \qquad
 (-1)^{h_{34}(y)}=s_3(y)s_4(y).
\]
Normalize the source at the unique stop on \(B_1\) and the target at
the unique stop on \(B_2\). Writing \(s_i=s_i(y)\), the source signs are
\(
 (1,s_1s_2,s_1s_3,s_1s_4)\),
while the signs of the target action of \(\alpha(y)\) are
\(
 (s_1s_2,1,s_1s_4,s_1s_3)\). They are intertwined by \(\pi=(12)(34)\). Before normalization, the
central corrections change the boundary-sign vector to
\((s_2,s_1,s_4,s_3)\) and act trivially on \(A_{\mathbb Q}\). The sign
at the target normalization point on \(B_2\) is therefore \(s_1\),
the same sign used to normalize the source at \(B_1\). The two
normalizations multiply the common absolute action by the same sign,
so the normalized absolute actions also agree.

On the non-trivial root blocks, the formulas for \(\phi\) act as the
inverses of the target signed cycles. Signed reversal conjugates each
cycle to its inverse. Together with \(\pi\), these reversals give an
integral intertwiner of the full stabilizer representations. The
ordinary homological action is unchanged, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:normalized-representation-extension} completes the
extension to \(\mathfrak R\).
